description:
This is our review of the NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU (using Founders Edition video card). Lots of people are talking about how the RTX 3090 "brings 8K gaming" to fruition. We put those claims to the test.
Grab a GN Foil 1 Million Subs shirt while you can! https://store.gamersnexus.net/products/limited-gold-foil-1-mill-subs-shirt (you get something cool, high quality, and get to support our further test equipment purchases at the same time. Thank you for 1 million subscribers! It's been a crazy ~13 years since we started the website, and a crazy 11 on YouTube).

Our RTX 3090 Founders Edition tear-down will go live later today, as will our overclocking livestream!

Here's our airflow photography of how the Founders Edition cooler behaves: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VVaGRtX80gI
Watch the RTX 3080 review here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oTeXh9x0sUc
RTX 3080 FE Tear-Down: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OX9Eh_NaC5c
Previous 3080 review article: https://www.gamersnexus.net/hwreviews/3618-nvidia-rtx-3080-founders-edition-review-benchmarks

Watch our NVIDIA Ampere GPU Architecture Deep-Dive: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AmNL2Cg2OO8
$13K of our New GPU Testing Methodology Equipment: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-P7-ML-bPCE

This benchmark of the NVIDIA RTX 3090 Founders Edition video card looks at thermal performance (temperatures), noise levels, surface flatness, contact pressure, gaming performance and benchmarks, and RTX ray tracing benchmarks. We also look at the "8K gaming is here" claims that NVIDIA made, particularly those that reached millions of people one day prior to launch. Additional testing will be done in the future for workstation benchmarks, like Blender Cycles rendering, Eevee real-time rendering, and Unreal Engine testing -- but the marketing claims go first, particularly given the tight timelines on the review turn-around. We'll also be overclocking the RTX 3090 in our RIPJAY contest revival, but that'll happen in a livestream later today (day of launch).

comments.text:
Years ago I went GCN gen 2 with the full compliment of 8gbs paritied across 2 GPUs. The compute was never reliably used except sort of in one game, ashes of the singularity. Hardware abstraction as I understand it isn't good enough to do what it could if you optimized per hardware in question by hand low level. 

5 plus years later, we are only beginning to see properish low level API implementation. Sold the shit out of that set up, which for its time was SUPERIOR to Maxwell and even Pascal on paper if we ignore lithography and memory generation. Planned obsolescence and market dominance to sway API adoption through various means. 

None of that was realized, until now, when im makeshift waiting for a proper replacement within the assumption the hardware was actually going to be used properly.

The GTX 1660 Ti shouldn't be faster than my old set up, but because software, it is. I bet it wouldnt be in resident evil 2 or 3 where even 1080P resolutions you can hit 13+ GBs, and this ignores raytracing injection, nor is it 8k. I get a lot of that is texture caching since there is streaming involved, but this will become the norm. The 3080 is already obsolete.

comments.text:
Im willing to bet for the performance per watt necessity and final parity with the competition, nvidia has given us true full scale stream processor function without serial based hardware optimizations. I think the holy grail was keeping the DX11 performance, which is what trashed GCN for years. But its all software limitation.

Remember the articles about GCN being optimized in hardware for low level APIs at the detriment of DX11? Well, nvidia was still doing that "faking" low level adoption on the shader side even during at least pascal. Load balance preemption means you get more efficient use of the one at the time but really fast method, its NOT asynchronous compute, but its a white lie I guess since no one cares. Dual math per pass, is technically asynchronous compute, but its not necessarily the same kind so who knows whats actually going on here. Would love some coverage.

That's not why they nuked it. They nuked it because wherever handled this release cycle either ignored a lot of basic things, is sabotaging them out didn't know what they were doing.
Take the 3080 partner boards. The min spec is a set of power circuit capacitors that are in the edge of their frequency response at the stock GPU frequencies. That's the spec most manufacturers used. Manufacturers that were also mistaken to not test this. But Nvidia give them an excuse by releasing an spec that doesn't work with "overclocking". All the while the ASUS, the founder's edition and a few others do use the proper capacitors that can handle the higher frequencies and respond to the EMI that level. They were so focused on cutting costs they ended up damaging their release. Dumb.
The principles for this are taught on a 201 level class. They should have known better and choose the right people for this. Marketing never know what they're doing except for brainwashing people.

comments.text:
Human perception of sharpness works linearly. So if we compare formats we have to compare one side in the aspect between formats and not the area number. 3840 has two times the sharpness (linearly) potential of 1920, but it has 4 times the area number in pixels.
If we call 7,680 by 4,320 8K, then that is 2 times the potential sharpness of 4K.
The amount of processing as well as requirements to storage capacity and bandwidth however relate to the area numbers.
1080p > 1440 > 2160 > 4320 in megapixels gives: 2.1 > 3.7  > 8.3 > 33.2 and this predicts the load on your PC

comments.text:
My thoughts for what its worth before I watch this video: 
I personally try to be on the bleeding edge of new tech to a degree where it makes sense. I was an LCD fanboy back in 1997, it was the future and it was clean and awesome. Same when widescreen was new and weird. It made sense. 4k fanboy for the last 7 years now. 4k movies and desktop back then was iffy but it was going to ramp up fast and the codecs and general infestructure of the internet was ample for it. These things were real advancements that became foundations of end-user computing/digital entertainment. 

But 8k? Im not seeing it for several more years. There is no fuckn need and I see any push for it right now as marketing bullshit that puts a bad taste in my mouth. At 6 feet, my 4k screen is nearly liquid smooth even at contrasting angles in games. At 4k I can still get 60fps+ in most games. Its the high-end sweetspot where the jump from 1440 is still a noticeable quality jump. Going to 8k the perception in quality is far far less for a massive performance penalty. Why? No way I would turn this on even if I had the option now. 8k movies? Yeah sure ill stream 60+GB for a single movie. No thanks unless i have a 110inch screen and im 10 feet from it. 

There comes a time when more resolution doesnt matter. It becomes the Ghz war. What matters is contrast ratio, color accuracy and fullfillment of color spec, refresh rate, response time, and other actualk meaningful things that are going o lag behind if we the consumers fall for 8K hype that is a decade too early to even start to be relevant or a good tradeoff.

comments.text:
There is one other class of customers who are interested in this card between gamers and workstation users: the extreme flight simulator crowd. These people often spend tens of thousands on custom rigs where the actual compute box is just the start. Multiple large monitors, specialized yokes, pedals and controls, special seats, etc are often the norm. I have a friend whom I've helped build such a rig and its been in various forms over the years. Currently it consists of 3 Samsung 65" 4K curved TVs for an immersive experience driven by an Asus X99 Broadwell-E mobo and Intel Core i&-6850K (6 core/12 thread) CPU (Corsair water cooled). It has 32 Gb of RAM, 1 TB of M2 boot storage and another 1 TB of secondary SSD storage. The graphics are dual Nvidia 1080 (not the ti that came later) from Gigabyte latched together in SLI. But SLI doesn't work all that well so we've been running it where one card drives all three displays and the other just runs physics.  Running X-Plane, we see about 20 fps on average which would suck for most gamers but my friend finds acceptable (he's been doing flight simming since MS Flight Sim II on the Apple ][ was a thing in the early 80s so his perspective is a little different).

Since this rig was built over three years ago (coming up on 4), I've been looking at upgrades for him that would make sense. Up until now, its worked well for him but we both felt it was time since we thought we could get a significant boost in fps (as opposed to incremental) and get extra features that will be useful down the road like 2nd gen ray tracing. Since he spent about $1500 on the two cards the last time, spending about the same money for a 3090 isn't out of the question.  Yes, we could remake the entire compute box but we'd like to start with the graphics first since it may be enough for his needs. His primary sim application is X-Plane but the new hotness right now is MS Flight Sim 2020. But it is still a work in progress and doesn't support three monitors just yet.

The attraction of the 3090 is that its about the money he wants to spend (past Titans at $2500 didn't make sense for the upgrade he'd get) and it comes with a boatload of VRAM which is extremely important in flight sims. Of course my problem is finding one for him since supply is rarer than anything in tech right now.

comments.text:
I'm sure that all 25 people in the world who have an 8k monitor/tv and want to game on it will jump at the chance to pickup a $1500 video card. I'm also sure that a bunch of "content creators" who have no real use for a $1500 video card will purchase it thinking it's going to save them "so much time" when in reality we are talking about 45 seconds here and 90 seconds there. So they are going to save themselves maybe 10 minutes a day. 

It's a halo product that has no reason to exist other than as a hedge against whatever AMD puts out being more powerful than the 3080. If Nvidia wasn't under possible threat of competition this card would have been the new TITAN and would have cost $2500+. The initial benchmarks show that the TITAN RTX outperforms it in several tasks and thats because Nvidia wants to sell their pro-grade cards to actual professionals who will be doing actual work. So they crippled the 3090 even after they called it the TITAN replacement. 

This is a card for a very specific group of people. This card is for folks with more money than sense first of all. They also have ambitions of being the next Dr. Disrespect or Shroud and making a living pro gaming. If that doesn't work out for them they will start playing with Blender and other programs then probably start making a bunch of youtube videos hoping for that Raid: Shadow Legends sponsorship for their channel. In the end probably 3/4 of the 3090 cards are going to be bought by parents for their teenage child who claims they need it for their future career but there is a 90% chance it will never do more than play minecraft with RTX on when they aren't still trying to become pro gamers/streamers/youtubers.

Real professionals who make a living doing serious work aren't going to be interested in the 3090 and will stick with pro cards. Sure those guys game but not on their production systems and they have a separate gaming PC at home.

comments.text: I think Doom Eternal's clustered forward rendering engine helped a ton for running at super high resolution, since forward rendering saves a lot of VRAM bandwidth and it capable to scale to all sorts of resolutions since every piece of data is local and almost always stays in L1 & L2 cache. Most other modern games are running a more or less "traditional" deferred rendering pipeline, not a tile-based one. Therefore it doesn't scale well with resolution, since in addition to taking more compute power to shade the pixels, you would also need an increase in per-core / group cache size which doesn't go up by that much (not 4x) than Turing.

I admit, I haven't played DOOM: Eternal, so if it's signficantly different than DOOM 2016 I'll admit my mistake, but I'm getting tired of people acting like DOOM 2016 (and presumably Eternal) are just fantastically well-coded and well-optimized games, when in fact they are quite probably the least demanding major AAA games of this generation.

In other words, of course they get high framerates -- there's nothing going on in the games. There's no physics, no environmental interactions, no environmental destruction, no AI routines to speak of, no NPCs, no huge outdoor environments like so many modern AAA games....There is a LOT less to process, it's that simple.

I'm not saying that they aren't well-coded and -optimized, but that's the only thing anyone thinks of, and it's only part of the story. People look at the framerate and the framerate alone, and don't take into account what's actually being produced each frame.

We're 13 years out from Crysis (2007), and still it seems like hardly anyone has learned the difference between well-optimized/not well-optimized and demanding/non-demanding.

comments.text:
​ @termitreter6545  I'm afraid you have several misconceptions:

"I mean, what game is technically very demanding, but is also well optimized?"

Crysis (2007). Crysis is possibly the most well-coded and -optimized PC FPS ever made. It's incredible what was accomplished--game logic, physics, AI, lighting, sounds, etc.--on a single-core Pentium. And despite the misinformation that persists, I fully maxed the game 8 months after release on a GTX 260. Did I get 60 fps at 1920x1200? Not even close. I could have, if I had wanted to drop lots of settings. But I didn't. The fact that there's such a massive difference in framerate between lowest & highest settings (unlike typical toss-ports) is one of the indications that it's well-coded and -optimized.

Also, let's remember: In 2007, 60 fps had not yet become a de facto standard. That didn't happen until after the Great Consolization of 2008, when GPUs kept getting faster, but we kept getting the same 360 console ports. Also, regarding resolution, the ReadMe of F.E.A.R. from 2005 calls anything above 1024x768 "high resolutions", and warns players from using them on (then) current-gen cards. I'm just trying to remind people of the standards of the day.

Crysis is unfortunately not multithreaded, but that is entirely different than being poorly coded or poorly optimized. It is extremely well-optimized for it's time, and for single-core systems.

"When those games run well, "

High (or acceptable) framerates is not the same thing as running well. As you point out, a poorly-coded game can get high framerates if it's old enough, and/or you throw enough power at it. It's certainly not running well, though.

"I know GTA5 is often used as an example, but lets be honest:"

It's used as an example because for a console port it IS fairly well-coded and -optimized. It's relative. No, it doesn't run near as well as it would if it was coded for the ground up for PC architecture, but it certainly delivers a LOT more at MUCH higher framerates than most console ports of this gen. Let's face it, it's just all-around a much better PC port than we were used to getting. Too bad it was a Rockstar anomaly.

"Thats a game originally made for PS3+XBox360, which were some of the weakest consoles we ever had in terms of gaming performance at release date."

That's actually the opposite of reality. The 360 was the most powerful MS console on release, giving many PCs a run for their money for a year or two, at least regarding CPU/GPU power. The One was a joke in comparison.

"Cutting down on super-demanding systems has always been part of optimization. Due you need that much physics? Does AI need to be super accurate with 500m distant NPCs?"

That's not true. Optimization means only reducing the processing budget required to accomplish something. Reducing what you're actually accomplishing is not optimization, it's degradation. In reality, it's acceptable to slightly reduce a feature if it means a far higher reduction in processing power, but that quickly becomes degradation if not checked.

"Youre also using a bad term with demanding. A game being demanding just means it needs a lot of processing power. It doesnt mean the game subjectively justifies its requirements to you"

Yes, 'demanding' means 'requiring a lot of processing power' by default. But you're confused. If a game doesn't justify the processing power it uses, it's not demanding -- because it doesn't actually demand that processing power. I can write a program that maxes a CPU with a black screen. It's not demanding, it's just a poorly-coded or useless program, that's all.

comments.text: 4:05 8K is not a bs moniker. It describes what it is, the number of columns of pixels in the display. The problem is the main aspect ratio of visual media, and therefore what tv and most monitor makers use is 16:9. 2K is 1920x1080, because 1.9K is stupid. 4K is double the width (and height, to keep 16:9 ratio) of 2K, 3840x2160. 8K is another doubling of each dimension, 7680x4320. As you can see, because it is keeping 16:9 aspect ratio, the more accurate names are 1.9K to 3.8K to 7.7K, they just round to single integers. It has nothing to do with the total number of pixels, and each doubling of K is quadrupling the total pixels.

comments.text:
In 16:9 space:
1080 x 1920 = 2K
2160 x 3840 = 4K
4320 x 7680 = 8K
8640 x 16360 = 16K
List goes on, saying 8K isn't 8K cus 7680 is not 8000 is silly as then 4K and 2K are themselves not what they say they are, only closer. This naming scheme is just to show the scale difference of which each step up is twice the horizontal and vertical resolution and 4 times the overall resolution of the prevous step.
1440 x 2560 = 2.5K
2880 x 5120 = 5K
5760 x 10240 = 10K etc as another reference of a K naming scheme.
If the scale wasn't consistant then you couldn't quickly tell the scale differnce of 1/4 or 4 times or 16 times etc. Naming scheme is perfectly fine.
If you see 4K, you know it's 4 times the resolution of 1080p or 2K, if you see 8K, you know that it's 4 times the resolution of 4K. If you want it to be more accurate, then just state the actual resolution.

comments.text:
@rotor13  DLSS 2.0 is completely indistinguishable from native and in some cases produces a higher fidelity. The AI is getting that good. I can't wait to see what DLSS 3.0 is capable of.

You really dumbed down how DLSS upscaling works.

The neural network is trained by Nvidia using "ideal" images of video games of ultra-high resolution on supercomputers and low resolution images of the same games. The result is stored on the video card driver. It is said the Nvidia uses DGX-1 servers to perform the training of the network.
The Neural Network stored on the driver compares the actual low resolution image with the reference and produce a full high resolution result. The inputs used by the trained Neural Network are the low resolution aliased images rendered by the game engine, and the low resolution, motion vectors from the same images, also generated by the game engine. The motion vectors tell the network which direction objects in the scene are moving from frame to frame, in order to estimate what the next frame will look like.

comments.text:
But... Did they fumble? I mean I'm kind of looking at it from their perspective. You're right it's not an 8k gaming card... But marketing as a "gaming card" when you can indeed get more performance out of it for gaming, it's priced only a few hundred more than the 2080 ti which consumers showed they'd buy for gaming (Albeit a small portion of the market), and when it's being made in partner model variants with increased voltage, and is now the primary target for a lot of Extreme Over clockers INSTEAD of the 3080 makes me think they not only knew exactly what they were doing, but in fact are going to get huge benefit out of this marketing. 

Interestingly I think the old "Titan" moniker hurt them a lot more then it ever helped them. It made people who were buying the 80 ti models feel like they were getting the "best of the best" when really they were getting the second best. It's not like they were getting the "best value" with 80 ti models either, that's always clearly and overwhelmingly belonged to the 60 or 70 series cards, so there is absolutely no way that Titan didn't create an arbitrary line that made it easier for people to justify getting the "best" when they really hadn't. 

By making the name change people who have to have the best won't compromise anymore the way they used to, instead they'll swing for what used to be a titan but is now a higher number, so seems to be part of the series. And it's not just the "people" or "consumers" who bought into this narrative, so did the partners. Whereas in the past partner variants didn't exist for Titans for the most part, they're coming out of the woodworks now, showing more emphasis on this marketing strategy. 

I will say if higher resolution VR headsets come out that eliminate the Screen Door effect, this might be a worthy card to power something like that. VR games tend to be more optimized because resolution and framerate matters more, so you might well be able to push 4k each eye 120hz and eliminate most of the motion sickness and screen door effect on a single card. In addition this is the only card that still supports SLI, and there has been talk (But little action admitably) for a long time of one card per eye implementation of SLI for VR, which would make this the "ultimate" VR setup, and the only option for such an SLI configuration.

Is it worth the money? Not for someone who needs to ask that question, no. However, for the large number of Middle Class and Upper Middle Class people who can afford thousands of dollars a year thrown at their hobby (Which may not be the majority of "gamers" but IS the majority of the consumer market, just by the definition of what Middle class means, and Middle class does include a LOT of people making 6-figure salaries), it totally makes sense, just as much as it does for fishing hobbyists who buy boats and sonar, or dirt-bike/quad hobbyists who buy that shit, or cross-country vacationers, or cruise enthusiasts, or people who do golf getaways... This isn't the life of the super-elite and wealthy, people just don't have perspective on what Middle Class really is until they get there...

comments.text:
The problem with the 3090 as a workstation card is that a lot of workstation workloads scales well to multi-GPU (even without an SLI bridge).  It's not uncommon to have 4 or even 8 GPUs in a workstation.  Cards like the Titan were made with this in mind.  But the 3090 is both huge and a power hog.  You cannot physically fit 8 3090s in any cases I know of, and even if you could the power requirements would be ridiculous.  Also the way the blow-through heatsink works seems particularly bad for multi-GPU setups.

Even if they had to clock it lower to do it, a physically smaller card that consumes less power would make a lot more sense for the workstation market.  You do still want the memory, as lots of memory is essential for a lot of workstation tasks.  But the 3090 seems to be made to emphasize single GPU performance at the expense of having workable multi-GPU setups.

In short this is being marketed as a gaming card because it's a bad workstation card...

I'm going to go out on a limb here and claim that price-to-value is not linear and should not be treated as such.
One grand you will get a pretty good violin. The 10m Stradivarius will not be 10,000 times better. 
For professional streamers the extra 120 percent spending may be worth the 2-10% increase in performance, the per hour price for one year of usage will be c. 75 cents. For this price they can get marginally better, which would otherwise take hundreds of hours of practice. In Warzone while sniping some objects take a second or more to render which may be life or death. Getting out of flow due to rendering constraints at the beginning of an 8 hours stream due may not be worth saving USD 3.2. 
That being said the biggest win for us casual gamers is the secondhand 2080 TIs on the market thanks to the 3080 and 3090 releases.

comments.text: Very weird marketing from Nvidia.  I think their 8K claim is heavily based on the ability to use DLSS 2.0, i.e. it's 8K in the sense that each of the pixels on an 8K screen get a different color value, but the caveat is that 8 out of every 9 of those pixels are totally made up (upscaled from 1440p).  Ultimately, games choose a lot of hacks in the interest of speed, so I don't have a major problem with this sort of marketing ... it's hacks all the way down.  It just seems silly to me to use this as a selling point when no gamer has an 8K monitor.  And, the whole "real time raytracing" thing is bullshit.  You can do an OptiX cycles render in Blender at 8k.  It ain't real-time my dudes.  It is fast, and each card is an upgrade in productivity for people that do 3d modeling and rendering on their workstations... but the accurate marketing would be "we added some more cores.  if you could use a few more cores on your graphics card, give us money."

comments.text: It's referred to as 4K because of the horizontal number of pixels. 3840 x 2160 pixel option (technically that is 3.8K, but saying 4K is easier). Same with 8K it is shorthand for 7.6K of horizontal pixel count. Yes the pixel count is different by more than twice, but the accepted syntax for it has been established.  When we went from 1080p to 4K the accepted moniker changed. 1920x1080 was 2K, but nobody called it that in the consumer market. 8K and 4K, from what I have seen these resolutions refer solely to the horizontal pixels. Its not whether 4K is twice the pixels of a 2K display. So unless you are going to argue 4K is not fully 4000 pixels in width as the reason its not 4K or 8K not being fully 8K pixels in width, then it should not really matter.

There is a lot more detail about it here:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4K_resolution

Its also why VR headsets are referred to by their pixel width. So the Quest 2 has a 2K per eye, and the headset itself is a 4K headset. Its not an especially useful term for VR headsets though since there is the matter of the field of view and such.

comments.text:
The statement that DLSS doesn't count when looking at 8K gaming grates on my ears. While I understand what you mean, that the use of DLSS means the card will render at least some parts of the scenes in a lower resolution and then use "smart" scaling using AI to blow up the result to full resolution, thus cheating to provide a higher frame rate. But at the same time I think the real issue should not be if a feature "cheat" to provide better performance but rather if the image quality suffers.

With the original DLSS implementations that was certainly a given. Enabling it resulted in image quality tanking hard, so in that case enabling DLSS certainly invalidates the claim that it should be used for bench marking those titles. However with DLSS 2.0 there was a lot of improvement regarding the image quality. Some people even claimed it improved image quality in at least two games, Control and some other I can't remember the name of. Now while I own Control I haven't tested DLSS at all so I can't claim to know that those claims are true, however in my opinion IF they are true, and the IQ is at least as good with DLSS 2.0 enabled as it is with it disabled, then I think enabling DLSS in that title is valid for benchmarking on cards supporting the option.

So, IMHO, features like DLSS should not summarily be dismissed for benchmarking, but rather evaluated on a game to game basis. If it can be considered to be invisible to the user, or even improving visual fidelity then it should also be used for benchmarks. And if it makes things look worse then it shouldn't be used for benchmarks. 

Yea, it complicates things, but I think that both Nvidia and AMD, and perhaps in the future sometime Intel, has to be given the chance to implement new tricks without having them summarily rejected as cheating. After all it we are going to look at it that way then every 3D GPU or 3D accelerator all the way back are cheating. They all use tricks to simplify the rendering, approximating the results that advanced mathematical algorithms run on a CPU can achieve, just very slowly, and so they "cheat" in order to achieve playable frame rates.

Back in the 1990's I played with a 3D render software that could do ray tracing, handled a huge number of reflections, soft shadows, global lighting and spot lights with directional lighting, refraction in different materials and a lot of things I can't possibly remember or had any chance of actually understanding. It rendered the scenes using nothing but the CPU and it could take days or even weeks to complete a single render. None of the graphics cards on the market can render a scene in a game engine that looks as good as that old software could, so doesn't that mean they are all cheating? ;^)

​ @martinarscott3524  Yeah, but there's a reason Doom Eternal runs well at 8K.

We have to ask, why do other games run so poorly at 8k? I suspect the answer lies primarily with the overall optimization of the game, the graphics API used, and of course the graphical fidelity of the game.

I understand that 8K gaming is used for marketing purposes, but Doom Eternal does run well at 8K, so dismissing it outright is ridiculous. Maybe we should be looking at what other games are doing wrong, rather than saying the 3090 isn't really capable of 8k gaming. I imagine that settings are played around with to achieve 60 fps, but honestly, would you say having to play on tweaked settings to play 4k at 60fps on a 1080ti means that the 1080ti isn't capable of 4k gaming?

It's not just a statistic, it's proof that 8k gaming at 60 fps is possible on a graphically impressive title. So why does Doom Eternal run so well?? That's the real question!

EDIT: And will video games in the future make better use of the power modern hardware has to offer, especially with the new Unreal Engine 5 coming next year?

comments.text:
I wonder how that new smaller power connector will go in a normal room (no AC) running at high load for quite some time. The connector may have 12 pins, but the wires have to be smaller to fit the connector (the connector for 12 pins is barely the size of 1x 8Pin). For me I would be worried that the high power draw if allowed to run non-stop for hours would potentially start to melt the wires. There were some crypto miner asics way back who tried to force 400W down a 6-Pin PCIe connector with 12AWG solder points, but the PSUs only ever used 16AWG or sometimes 14AWG if lucky on the top quality ones. The net result of that was basically the equipment setting itself on fire due to too much current passing through the 16AWG wires (even when using the special 12AWG 1x 6Pin to 2x 8Pin adapter). I know though (at least on the 3080) they are using larger flat style connections from the connector to the PCB, but that was never the issue on those ASICs that pulled 400W into the plug (even though Molex had rated this particular plug at 450W, it was only rated like that for 3 minutes full load, 30 minutes rest in cycles), the issue was the plug itself with the plastic catching on fire and sometimes the wires leading into the plug.

One thing I am interested to find out is what is the thickness of the +12v wires on the 12-pin connector and can it really keep up with high power draw for hours on end?



Ohh wait... Never mind... It's only a gaming card... People wouldnt possibly want to load the card to those extremes for hours on end.

"Why, NVIDIA? Why did you do it?"

Anchoring. If you promote the 3090 as a workstation card, then the gaming market might see a base model 3070 and a high end model 3080, which sends the average consumer to the 3070 as the "cheap and almost as good as the best" option and the premium buyers to the 3080. 

By having all models "gaming", then you give the appearance of a low end 3070, base model 3080 and high end 3090. That makes the 3080 more popular to general audiences as a speed/cost sweet point and opens up the 3090 to the very high-end gaming purchasers (along with the CAD people who would buy it regardless).
